The body names the capability in its `capability` field, using the same word `GET /v1/api/capabilities` publishes, so a caller can read the capability set once and stop asking rather than retrying a refusal that will never change.

endpoints.doc: Search individual steps rather than whole runs. This is how you answer 'which tool call is slow' or 'show me every call to this model that errored', across every trace at once.

query.name: q
query.doc: Full-text search across name, input and output.

query.name: min_duration_ms
query.doc: Only spans at least this slow.

endpoints.doc: Log search, filtered by minimum severity, text, time window, trace and span. Because logs carry trace ids, every result links straight to the run that produced it.

query.name: q
query.doc: Full-text search across the message and structured fields.

query.name: order
query.doc: `asc` or `desc`. Defaults to `desc`, newest first, which is where an investigation starts.

endpoints.summary: Query a metric as a time series
endpoints.doc: Aggregates raw points into time buckets and returns a series per label combination. Supports sum, count, mean, min, max and quantiles, so a chart is one request rather than a client-side fold over raw points.

query.name: bucket
query.doc: Bucket width, such as `1m`, `5m`, `1h`. Chosen automatically when omitted.

query.name: group_by
query.doc: Label keys to split the series on.

query.name: filter
query.doc: Label equality filters, as `key:value` pairs joined by commas: `model:gpt-4o,status:ok`. A point matches when every named label has that value. A colon, not `=`, so the value needs no escaping in a query string. A key cannot contain `:` or `,`, and a value cannot contain `,`. A JSON object here matches no point, and the answer is an empty series.

endpoints.doc: Every machine evaluation, filterable by scorer, source, run, experiment, value range and time.

query.name: experiment_id
query.doc: Only scores recorded by this experiment.

endpoints.doc: Records a machine evaluation against a span or a trace. Supply `min` and `max`: a bare number with no declared scale cannot be compared to anything.
Records a person's judgement of a run or a step. Call this from your own product's thumbs-up control and the judgement lands on the exact trace that produced the answer.

The human judgements on one run, read from the trace detail. `trace_id` is required and is refused when absent: mcpd cannot yet list a whole project's feedback, and answering an empty list instead would read as though nobody had judged anything. Every other parameter is refused by name as well, so a filter this endpoint does not apply cannot come back as a plausible wrong answer.

query.name: trace_id
query.doc: The run whose judgements to read. Required.

endpoints.summary: Headline numbers for a time window
endpoints.doc: Run count, error rate, latency quantiles, token totals and cost for a window, optionally split by a dimension. One request backs the overview screen.

query.name: from
query.doc: Start of the window. Defaults to 24 hours before `to`.

query.name: to
query.doc: End of the window. Defaults to now.

endpoints.doc: Spend over a window, split by model, provider, entity, environment, status, session, user, service or run name, with token detail behind each figure. Answers 'where is the money going' without exporting to a spreadsheet.

query.name: from
query.doc: Start of the window. Defaults to seven days before `to`.

query.name: to
query.doc: End of the window. Defaults to now.

query.name: bucket
query.doc: Time bucket for a series, such as `1h` or `1d`. Omit for totals only.

endpoints.doc: Every scorer mcpd ships, with what it measures and whether it needs configuration. Scorers are deterministic code, not model calls, so they cost nothing to run and give the same answer twice.

Scores runs that are already stored, and records the results. Naming a scorer that does not exist fails the request before any work happens; a scorer that cannot answer on a given run is reported in `skipped` rather than failing it.
Reports the per-scorer delta between two experiments beside the sample size on each side, and refuses to call a comparison decidable below twenty observations.
Every dataset in the project, with its case count.
A dataset is a named set of cases to run a version of an agent against. Leave `dataset_id` empty and mcpd assigns one.

endpoints.summary: List the cases in a dataset
endpoints.doc: The cases themselves, each with its input, its expected answer when it has one, and the run it was captured from.
Adds cases written by hand or exported from somewhere else. Leave each `item_id` empty and mcpd assigns one.

Turns runs that already happened into permanent cases. This is what datasets are for: the run that went wrong in production on Tuesday becomes a regression test that every later version has to pass, and it keeps its trace id, so the case always points back at the run it came from.

query.name: project
query.doc: Which project the runs are in.

endpoints.doc: Every recorded run of a dataset against a version of an agent.
Registers a run of a dataset so its scores can be compared against another version later. Scores recorded with this experiment's id are what `compare` reads.
Returns 200 as long as the process is running. Wire this to a Kubernetes liveness probe. It never touches storage, so a slow database cannot cause a restart loop.
Returns 200 once storage is reachable and migrations have completed. Wire this to a Kubernetes readiness probe so traffic is not sent to an instance that cannot serve it.

mcpd's own counters in Prometheus text format: signals accepted, rejected, over quota and unbounded, duplicate batches, traces sampled out, ingest and query requests handled, request errors, audit rows that could not be written, and uptime. An observability tool that cannot be observed is a liability.

endpoints.summary: What this deployment's storage backend can do
endpoints.doc: The capability set of the store behind this daemon. mcpd has one storage trait and three backends, and they differ: discovery, delta polling, per-signal retention and case folding outside ASCII are not on all three. Read this once and offer only what the deployment answers, rather than discovering a difference from an empty list. An endpoint whose capability is false refuses with 501 and names the same field, so nothing here can disagree with what the daemon actually does.

Every recorded read of stored payloads and every deletion, newest first. Writing an audit row never fails the request it describes: a row that cannot be written is logged and counted as `mcpd_audit_write_failures_total` on `/metrics`, and the read still returns.

query.name: project
query.doc: Which project to read. Defaults to the account's own project for an account credential, else the daemon's default project.

query.name: action
query.doc: Only rows recording this action, such as `delete_trace`.

endpoints.summary: Erase everything recorded about one person
endpoints.doc: Removes every run in the project attributed to this user, with the spans, logs, metrics, scores and feedback attached to those runs, and any log line recorded against the user on its own. On a daemon that serves durable runs, it also removes every ended run whose correlation carries this `user_id`, with its whole tree of subworkflow runs and everything stored for them; a run that has not ended is counted in `runs_in_flight` and left whole. This answers a deletion request in one call, instead of finding each run by hand and deleting it trace by trace. Only the project in the request is touched, and only if the key reaches it: the same user id in a project the key cannot open is left alone and is not counted, so a count can never disclose that the subject exists elsewhere. Returns a count per signal, so the reply to the person can say what went. The erasure is recorded in the audit log.

params.name: user_id
params.doc: The person to erase, written as the `user_id` your instrumentation set on the run. Send it as you sent it at ingest; the daemon applies the same hashing it applied then.

query.name: project
query.doc: Which project to erase within. Defaults to the account's own project for an account credential, else the daemon's default project.

endpoints.doc: Stores one version of a definition. The canonical body is the document with sorted keys and no insignificant whitespace, minus `version`. An identical body already stored is confirmed at its version rather than stored again, so posting the same code twice is a no-op, and a version is immutable once stored. A body the definition schema refuses is a 400 naming the field.

query.name: project
query.doc: Which project. A selector: refused with 403 on a mismatch with the key's grant, filled in for a single-project key, and a 400 when a multi-project key names none.

409.doc: A stored version holds a different body under the number you named. A stored version never changes: post the body under a new version, or leave `version` absent and let the daemon assign one.

endpoints.doc: Every stored version of every definition in the project, with its body.

query.name: project
query.doc: Which project. A selector: refused with 403 on a mismatch with the key's grant, filled in for a single-project key, and a 400 when a multi-project key names none.

endpoints.doc: One definition. Without `version`, the highest stored version, which is the one a run started now would pin.

query.name: project
query.doc: Which project. A selector: refused with 403 on a mismatch with the key's grant, filled in for a single-project key, and a 400 when a multi-project key names none.

query.name: version
query.doc: Which version. Absent means the highest stored.

404.doc: No definition with that id in the project, or none at the named version.

endpoints.doc: Starts a run and answers it as stored. The run row, its trace id, its first cursor and everything that cursor requires commit in one transaction, so a 200 means the first step is already on disk for a worker to claim. With `idempotency_key`, a repost within 24 hours answers the same run and starts nothing.

404.doc: No definition with that id in the project, or none at the named version.

endpoints.doc: Runs in the project, newest first.

query.name: project
query.doc: Which project. A selector: refused with 403 on a mismatch with the key's grant, filled in for a single-project key, and a 400 when a multi-project key names none.

query.name: cursor
query.doc: Opaque cursor from a previous page.

endpoints.summary: Get one run with its journal
endpoints.doc: One run with every attempt at every step, and the deadlines and waits it currently holds.

404.doc: No run with that id in a project the key reaches.

endpoints.doc: Ends the run and every child under it as `cancelled`: their deadlines and waits are deleted and every live attempt is marked `failed`. A worker holding a lease learns on its next call, with a 409 `run_terminal`. A parent of a cancelled child sees the child's step fail and follows its `on_error`, unless the parent itself was the run cancelled. Cancelling a run that has already ended changes nothing and still answers 200. The body is empty.

404.doc: No run with that id in a project the key reaches.

endpoints.doc: The run's event log after a sequence number. Send `Accept: text/event-stream` and the same route answers server-sent events instead: one frame per row with `id` set to `seq`, held open until the run ends or you disconnect. `after` is the reattach point in both forms.

query.name: after
query.doc: Return rows with a sequence number greater than this. Exclusive; the default returns the log from its first row.

query.name: limit
query.doc: The most rows to return in one page.

404.doc: No run with that id in a project the key reaches.

endpoints.doc:
Walks backwards from one step of a run along the data dependencies its definition declares, and returns the ancestors whose output that step consumed.

A workflow template such as `${steps.classify.output.kind}` is an explicit edge from one step to another, written in the document the run pinned at start, so the chain is read out of the definition rather than guessed from timing or from what happened to run first. The answer names the case a status code cannot: an ancestor that ended `succeeded`, with every step between it and the failure green as well, whose value the failure consumed anyway.

The step key is a query parameter rather than a path segment because a key may contain a slash, as `refund/issue` does, and an encoded slash inside a path segment is rewritten or refused by enough proxies to make it a bad contract.

query.name: step
query.doc: The step key to explain, exactly as the journal keys it, such as `refund/issue` or `poll[7]/classify`.

query.name: max_depth
query.doc: How far back to walk. The walk stops there and sets `truncated`, so a long chain, a loop or a definition that reads its own earlier steps repeatedly cannot produce an unbounded answer.

404.doc: No run with that id in a project the key reaches, or the run's definition declares no step with that key.

endpoints.summary: Deliver an event to one run
endpoints.doc: Delivers an event to one run by id. The daemon reads the run's open wait on `event`, takes its key, and routes the event as the publish endpoint would, with the same deduplication.

404.doc: No run with that id, or the run holds no open wait on that event.

endpoints.doc: Delivers an event to whichever run is waiting for it, matched on project, event name and key. Delivery writes the payload as the waiting step's output and moves the run in the same transaction. With no run waiting, the event is parked for 24 hours, and the next run that reaches a matching wait with `accept_parked` consumes it, oldest first.

Stores the definitions a worker serves and tells it the lease timings. Nothing about the worker itself is stored: dispatch reads the runnable set, never a worker table, so a worker that dies needs no deregistration.

409.doc: A stored version holds a different body under the number you named. A stored version never changes: post the body under a new version, or leave `version` absent and let the daemon assign one.

endpoints.doc: Long-polls for runnable steps, up to `wait_ms`. A step is runnable when it has a `pending` attempt whose retry timer, if any, has fired, its run and its root are `running`, no other attempt of the same step is live or inside its reclaim window, and neither the run nor its root has spent `max_steps` or `max_cost_usd`. A run refused for a spent ceiling is ended `failed` with an error naming the ceiling.

endpoints.summary: Declare that a step body is about to run
endpoints.doc: Moves the attempt from `leased` to `started`, extends the lease and closes an open reclaim window. Required under `at_most_once`: post it, wait for the 200, then run the body. Optional under `at_least_once`, where skipping it only means a crash mid-body is recorded in the journal as a requeue rather than in the trace as an error on that attempt. The body is empty.

404.doc: No lease with that id.

409.doc: The lease is no longer the one that may act on this attempt, or the run has ended. `reason` says which, and what to do next.

endpoints.doc: Extends the lease. Post it every `heartbeat_ms` while the body runs, whether or not `started` was posted. `reclaimed` is true when the call found the attempt `orphaned` and restored it to the state it came from. The body is empty.

404.doc: No lease with that id.

409.doc: The lease is no longer the one that may act on this attempt, or the run has ended. `reason` says which, and what to do next.

endpoints.doc: Ends an attempt with an output. In one transaction the attempt becomes `succeeded`, `state` is merged shallowly into the run, `usage` is priced and charged to the attempt, the run and the root, the step's deadlines are deleted, the closing span is enqueued, and once every slot the cursor requires has ended the cursor advances and everything the next position requires is written.

404.doc: No lease with that id.

409.doc: The lease is no longer the one that may act on this attempt, or the run has ended. `reason` says which, and what to do next.

endpoints.doc: Ends an attempt with an error. `class` decides what follows: `retryable` writes a retry timer while attempts remain, at the node's backoff or `retry_after_ms` if that is larger; `unservable` returns the attempt to `pending` after one lease length without spending the retry budget; every other class applies the node's `on_error` at once, as does a `retryable` failure with no attempts left. `fail_run` ends the run `failed` with the message; `continue` marks the step `failed` and advances.

404.doc: No lease with that id.

409.doc: The lease is no longer the one that may act on this attempt, or the run has ended. `reason` says which, and what to do next.

endpoints.doc: Every configured monitor the key reaches, with the condition it is latched in and its most recent reading. A monitor names the project it watches and carries the webhook it posts to, so the list is filtered by the key's project grant rather than returned whole. Monitors are configured in the daemon's configuration file, so there is nothing to create here.

Acknowledges a tripped monitor. Acknowledging silences the transition without pretending the condition cleared: the monitor stays `acknowledged` while it still breaches, and returns to `nominal` on its own when the number recovers. Acknowledging a monitor that is not tripped changes nothing. The body is empty. A key that does not reach the project the monitor watches is refused with `403`, naming the monitor rather than the project that owns it.

404.doc: No monitor with that id.

endpoints.doc: Every configured service level objective the key reaches, filtered by the key's project grant the way the monitor list is. Objectives are configured in the daemon's configuration file, so there is nothing to create here.

Acknowledges a tripped objective, under the same latching rule as a monitor: it stays `acknowledged` while the burn rate still breaches, and returns to `nominal` when it recovers. The body is empty. The project grant is checked the way it is on a monitor acknowledgement.

404.doc: No objective with that id.

endpoints.summary: The aspects a project describes traces along
endpoints.doc:
Every aspect this project has, with the bounds a clustering pass runs under.

An aspect is an axis. Four ship with the daemon: `goal` is what the user wanted, `sentiment` is the tone they expressed, `behaviour` is what the agent did about it, and `outcome` is how the interaction ended. They are ordinary rows rather than a list compiled into a client, so nothing can hold a second opinion about what exists.

`outcome` ships derived, which means the daemon writes its notes itself from the run's status, the step error class, the silent producer flag on the cause report and the divergence watch, with no model anywhere. A deployment that has configured nothing therefore fills one aspect on its own, which is enough to see the whole pipeline work before a model is wired to anything.

endpoints.summary: The entities that have aspect notes
endpoints.doc:
Which agents, workflows and tools have enough recorded to be worth opening, and which are still filling up.

A row appears as soon as the first note about an entity is recorded, before any theme exists. That is deliberate: an empty screen with a count moving on it is a different thing from an empty screen, and a reader has to be able to tell them apart.

Every roll-up here is computed and none of it is optional, because mcpd serves one version of itself and has no older server to tolerate.

query.name: cursor
query.doc: Opaque cursor from a previous page.

501.doc: This deployment's storage backend does not implement what this endpoint needs. The body names the capability in its `capability` field, using the same word `GET /v1/api/capabilities` publishes as `theme_analysis`, so a caller can read the capability set once and stop asking rather than retrying a refusal that will never change.

endpoints.summary: How far the pipeline has got for one entity
endpoints.doc:
The honest empty state. For one entity: how many of its traces carry notes, and per aspect how many notes exist, what state that aspect is in, and how many more notes it needs before a clustering pass will run. Every number is counted from stored rows, so nothing here is an estimate of what is coming.

An aspect reads `collecting` below the floor of 50 notes, `processing` once it has them and no snapshot covers it yet, and `ready` when one does. Read this before concluding that a themes screen is broken: the three states look identical on screen and mean different things.

query.name: entity_kind
query.doc: The kind of entity to read. An entity is the pair of a kind and a name, which is the identity spans already carry.

404.doc: No entity of that kind and name in a project this key reaches.

501.doc: This deployment's storage backend does not implement what this endpoint needs. The body names the capability in its `capability` field, using the same word `GET /v1/api/capabilities` publishes as `theme_analysis`, so a caller can read the capability set once and stop asking rather than retrying a refusal that will never change.

endpoints.doc:
The timeline. Each snapshot is one clustering pass over a moving window of notes, and every theme query names exactly one of them.

There are two presentations. `inventory` returns consecutive snapshots for a caller walking the series. `landmarks` returns a bounded, time balanced selection across the whole range, with the oldest and the newest snapshot in that range always included and the rest sampled by time, which is what a timeline of a couple of dozen points needs; each row then says which of the two reasons put it there.

Windows overlap. Two snapshots describe overlapping sets of traces, so their counts must never be added together.

query.name: entity_kind
query.doc: The kind of entity to read. An entity is the pair of a kind and a name, which is the identity spans already carry.

query.name: aspects
query.doc: Only snapshots that cover all of these aspects. Unset means every snapshot for the entity, whatever it covers.

query.name: presentation
query.doc: `inventory` for consecutive snapshots, `landmarks` for a time balanced selection across the range.

query.name: from
query.doc: Only snapshots whose cutoff falls at or after this. It bounds the range a landmark selection is drawn from as well as what is returned.

query.name: to
query.doc: Only snapshots whose cutoff falls before this.

query.name: limit
query.doc: How many snapshots to return, 1 to 100. A landmark selection of more than a couple of dozen points is more than a timeline can draw and more than a reader can scrub.

query.name: cursor
query.doc: Opaque cursor from a previous page.

404.doc: No entity of that kind and name in a project this key reaches.

501.doc: This deployment's storage backend does not implement what this endpoint needs. The body names the capability in its `capability` field, using the same word `GET /v1/api/capabilities` publishes as `theme_analysis`, so a caller can read the capability set once and stop asking rather than retrying a refusal that will never change.

endpoints.summary: Themes across two to four aspects at once
endpoints.doc:
The cross-aspect view: one stage per aspect, its nodes, and the links between neighbouring stages. A link's count is the number of traces assigned to both of its ends.

This shows association and not causation. A ribbon between a goal theme and an outcome theme means the two were written about the same runs. It does not mean one caused the other.

The order of `aspects` is meaningful and is not a display preference. Links only ever join neighbouring stages, so goal beside outcome answers a different question from goal beside behaviour, and asking for the same aspects in another order asks another question. Fewer than two aspects is refused by name rather than answered with an empty flow, because one stage has no links in it.

Each stage carries at most one noise node and at most one overflow node. Noise is the notes that joined no theme, and it is not a failure bucket: it is rare requests, wording nothing else matched and patterns that have not recurred yet, so a large noise share means varied traffic or too few notes. Overflow is everything past `theme_limit_per_stage`, folded into one node so the stage totals still add up.

query.name: entity_kind
query.doc: The kind of entity to read. An entity is the pair of a kind and a name, which is the identity spans already carry.

query.name: aspects
query.doc: Two to four aspect names, in the order the stages are wanted. The order changes the answer.

query.name: snapshot_id
query.doc: Which snapshot to read. Every count in the response belongs to this one window.

query.name: theme_limit_per_stage
query.doc: How many themes to return per stage, 1 to 100, before the rest are folded into the overflow node. The fold happens on the server because only the server knows what it truncated.

query.name: filter
query.doc: Drill in. Repeat as `filter=aspect:theme_id`, or `filter=aspect:noise`, up to four times with a different aspect each time. The daemon recomputes the counts and the shares over the traces that survive every filter, so the answer does not change shape with the size of the snapshot and a client never has to fetch the assignments and filter them itself.

404.doc: No such snapshot for that entity, or `aspects` names an aspect the project does not have.

501.doc: This deployment's storage backend does not implement what this endpoint needs. The body names the capability in its `capability` field, using the same word `GET /v1/api/capabilities` publishes as `theme_analysis`, so a caller can read the capability set once and stop asking rather than retrying a refusal that will never change.

endpoints.doc:
A theme's label, lifecycle state and counts in one snapshot, returned beside the snapshot's own counts so a caller can write `28 of 70 traces in this window` without a second request.

A theme this snapshot does not hold is a 200 with no theme rather than a 404. Scrubbing a timeline back past a theme's birth is a reasonable question, and the answer is that the theme was not there yet. The 404 is kept for a theme id this entity has never had, which is a different mistake and deserves a different answer.

params.name: theme_id
params.doc: The theme to read. `noise` is reserved and is not a theme: read a stage's noise from the flow.

query.name: entity_kind
query.doc: The kind of entity to read. An entity is the pair of a kind and a name, which is the identity spans already carry.

query.name: aspect
query.doc: Which aspect the theme was clustered along.

query.name: snapshot_id
query.doc: Which snapshot to read it in.

404.doc: No such snapshot, or a theme id this entity has never had. A theme that exists and is absent from this snapshot is a 200 with no theme.

501.doc: This deployment's storage backend does not implement what this endpoint needs. The body names the capability in its `capability` field, using the same word `GET /v1/api/capabilities` publishes as `theme_analysis`, so a caller can read the capability set once and stop asking rather than retrying a refusal that will never change.

endpoints.doc:
The sentences that put traces in this theme, each with the run it was written about, so a reader can go from a theme to the runs behind it.

Ordered by how much each note's wording overlaps the theme's label, most alike first, with the note id breaking a tie so the order is total and the same on every read and every replica.

Pass `noise` as the theme id to read the notes that joined no theme in this snapshot. There is no separate noise route: noise is a node in the flow and its notes are read here, because a second pair of routes returning an identically shaped answer would be two more rows in this reference and no new question answered.

The text is payload. This endpoint takes a read key, it is recorded in the audit ledger like every other endpoint that hands back what a user wrote, and the notes it returns are swept by retention and erased with their subject.

params.name: theme_id
params.doc: The theme to read, or `noise` for the notes in this snapshot that joined no theme.

query.name: entity_kind
query.doc: The kind of entity to read. An entity is the pair of a kind and a name, which is the identity spans already carry.

query.name: aspect
query.doc: Which aspect the theme was clustered along.

query.name: snapshot_id
query.doc: Which snapshot to read it in.

The daemon recomputes the counts and the shares over the traces that survive every filter, so the answer does not change shape with the size of the snapshot and a client never has to fetch the assignments and filter them itself.

The body names the capability in its `capability` field, using the same word `GET /v1/api/capabilities` publishes as `theme_analysis`, so a caller can read the capability set once and stop asking rather than retrying a refusal that will never change.

endpoints.doc:
Every stored snapshot that holds this theme, with its state, counts and coverage at each point, and the themes it split from, split into, merged from or merged into.

This is the only theme route that names no snapshot, because the series is the answer. Points come back oldest first, so nothing has to be reordered before it is drawn or differenced.

Retention bounds what can be answered. The oldest point returned is the oldest snapshot still stored, which is a lower bound on the theme's age and not necessarily its birth, so a series that starts at the edge of the window says when mcpd started looking rather than when the theme started.

Windows overlap, so read the points as a series and never add their counts together.

query.name: entity_kind
query.doc: The kind of entity to read. An entity is the pair of a kind and a name, which is the identity spans already carry.

query.name: aspect

endpoints.summary: What was written about one trace
endpoints.doc:
Every aspect note recorded about one trace, in catalogue order. A trace id crosses service boundaries, so two projects can each hold a run under it: name the project to read that one. Without it, the projects the key reaches are tried in order and the first that holds the trace answers.

Read it beside the trace itself. A note is the sentence that put this run in each of its themes, so it is the shortest route from a theme back to what happened, and it is also the place to check a theme you do not believe: a note proves a definition said this about the trace at a version, and the trace proves the rest.

An empty list is the ordinary answer for a recent trace. Writing a note lags ingestion.

endpoints.doc: Starts an account. The answer is the same whether or not the email already has an account, so it does not say which addresses are in use. A link is sent to the address: for a new account it confirms the address and logs in; for an address already in use it says so and offers a password reset. The account and its project are created now, and the session comes from opening the link. Limited per client address: a client that signs up too often is answered with 429 and a `Retry-After` header. Answers 404 when the daemon was not started with `--signup`, and 503 when it has no way to send mail.

endpoints.doc: Starts a session for an account. A wrong password and an unknown email get the same 401 with the same message, so the answer does not say which emails have accounts. With the right password, an account with two-step log-in on and no `totp_code` gets 401 with the code `totp_required`; an address not yet confirmed gets 403 and a new link; and a member of an organisation that enforces single sign-on gets 403 with the code `sso_required`. Limited per client address and per email. Answers 404 when the daemon has no accounts.

401.doc: The email and password do not match an account.

403.doc: The password is right, and the address is not confirmed yet or the organisation requires single sign-on.

404.doc: This daemon does not offer accounts.

429.doc: Too many attempts from this address or for this email. Wait for the number of seconds in `Retry-After`.
